experiments.title: Experiment 1: Baseline Efficiency & Scaling (Ideal Channel)
experiments.description: Evaluates raw sifting efficiency, distillable key yield, and simulator runtime scaling with pulse count under zero noise and zero eavesdropping.

experiments.title: Experiment 2: Depolarizing Noise Tolerance & Abort Thresholds
experiments.description: Quantifies the degradation of QBER and Bell parameter |S| as depolarizing noise increases, pinpointing the abort threshold for each protocol.

experiments.title: Experiment 3: Intercept-Resend Attack Detection Sensitivity
experiments.description: Evaluates the sensitivity of each protocol to quantum channel interception across intensities (0% to 100%) at baseline 2% depolarizing noise.

experiments.title: Experiment 4: Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) Attack & Classical Channel Authentication
experiments.description: Evaluates protocol behavior under full quantum channel interception with classical basis HMAC authentication enabled vs disabled.

experiments.title: Experiment 5: Finite-Key Statistical Convergence & Stability
experiments.description: Examines statistical variance, false alarm rates, and estimation stability across pulse counts under constant 3% depolarizing noise.

scorecard.E91: 11.1% per pair (1/9 basis coincidence; ~5.56% per physical photon)
scorecard.Simulation Takeaway: BB84 yields the highest raw sifted bits per emitted quantum pulse. In this E91 implementation, only 1 of 9 basis pairs is used for key extraction.
B92 aborts under modest channel noise due to non-orthogonal state overlap. BB84 and E91 tolerate higher depolarizing noise before aborting.
E91 validates quantum non-locality directly on pairs; however, full device-independent security in reality requires loophole-free experimental assumptions.

scorecard.BB84: Sifted Basis Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER)
scorecard.Simulation Takeaway: E91 detects Eve through the collapse of the Bell correlation parameter |S| even before classical key error analysis.
B92 requires fewer laser diodes; E91 requires distributing two synchronized photons per pair across two optical arms.
Quantum channels alone cannot prevent MitM attacks. Classical channel authentication (e.g. pre-shared HMAC) is strictly required across all three protocols.
